questions.question: What is the difference between a class and an object in Java?
questions.title: Class vs Object in Java
questions.direct_answer: A **class** is a blueprint that defines what data (fields) and behaviour (methods) a type will have. An **object** is a real, concrete instance created from that blueprint using `new`. One class can produce many independent objects, each with its own copy of the field values.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you understand that a class is a template and an object is a live instance — and that each object has its own independent data.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Using 'class' and 'object' interchangeably, or thinking all objects share the same field values.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention that the class defines memory layout once at compile time, but each object allocates its own heap memory at runtime — and only static fields are shared.

sections.title: A Class Is the Blueprint; an Object Is the Thing You Build From It
sections.content:
A **class** is a blueprint, and an **object** is a real, concrete thing built from that blueprint. That one sentence is the whole idea — everything else is just detail filling it in.

Why does Java separate the two? Because you almost always need many things of the same kind. You describe what a "student" looks like exactly once — a `name`, some `marks`, a way to print a grade — and then you stamp out as many real students as you need from that single description. **Writing the description once and reusing it** is the entire point.

Here is how it works, one idea at a time. A **class** is just text in your source file. When you write `class Student { ... }`, nothing is created in memory yet — it is a recipe written on paper. An **object** is what you get when you actually run that recipe using the `new` keyword: `new Student()` builds a real Student inside a region of memory called the **heap** (the area where Java keeps objects while your program runs). The classic picture is a cookie cutter and a cookie. The cutter (the class) defines the shape; each cookie (an object) is its own separate, edible thing.

The detail interviewers listen for: one class can build many objects, and each object owns its **own** copy of the data. Set `s1.marks = 95` and `s2.marks` is untouched — the two objects share the shape, not the values. The only exception is a `static` field, which belongs to the class itself and is shared by every object.

The gotcha that trips up beginners: writing `Student s;` does **not** create an object. It only creates an empty reference holding `null` (a pointer to nothing). The object exists only after you call `new` — miss that and your very next line throws a `NullPointerException`.

> **The rule:** a `class` is a compile-time blueprint that uses no memory, while an `object` is a live instance on the `heap` with its own data.

sections.title: One Class, Many Independent Objects
sections.content:
When you call `new` three times on the same class, three separate objects appear on the heap — each at its own address, each with its own field values. ```mermaid flowchart TD C["Student class
(blueprint — no heap memory)"] -->|"new Student()"| O1["s1 @ heap 0x100
name: Alice, marks: 95"] C -->|"new Student()"| O2["s2 @ heap 0x200
name: Bob, marks: 72"] C -->|"new Student()"| O3["s3 @ heap 0x300
name: Carol, marks: 88"] O1 -.->|"changing s1.marks
does NOT affect"| O2 ``` The class itself never appears on the heap — only the objects do. Each one is independent.

sections.title: Class and Objects in Practice
Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Using "class" and "object" as if they mean the same thing** — the class is the definition you write, the object is one live instance built from it; the interviewer hears the slip the moment you make it.
- **Assuming all objects of a class share their field values** — each object gets its own copy of the instance fields, so changing `s1.marks` never touches `s2.marks` unless that field is `static`.
- **Believing `Student s;` already creates an object** — it only creates a `null` reference; the object exists only after `new`, and touching `s` before that throws `NullPointerException`.
- **Thinking the class takes heap memory** — only objects live on the heap; the class is loaded once as a template, so "how many objects" and "how many classes" are completely different questions.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- A **class** is a compile-time template — defines fields and methods, allocates no heap memory.
- An **object** is a runtime instance — created with `new`, lives on the heap, has its own field values.
- **One class → many independent objects**: each holds its own copy of instance fields.
- Modifying one object never affects another (unless they share a `static` field).
- Declaring `Student s;` only creates a `null` reference — no object exists until you call `new`.

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content:
I'd frame it by **what each one actually is in memory**. A `class` is the description you write once — what fields and methods a `Student` should have — and on its own it **takes no memory** and isn't a real anything; it's just a template. An `object` is what you get when you run that description with `new`: a concrete `Student` living on the `heap` with its own data.

The thing people get wrong is **treating the two as interchangeable**, or assuming every object shares the same values. They don't — one class can stamp out hundreds of objects, and **each one owns its own copy** of the instance fields, so changing one student's `marks` leaves the others completely alone. The only thing they genuinely share is a `static` field, which belongs to the class itself.

The trap I'd call out is that just declaring `Student s` doesn't create anything — it's `null` until you actually call `new`. So the mental model I keep is **one blueprint, many independent things** built from it.

questions.question: What happens in memory when you create an object using the `new` keyword in Java?
questions.title: What `new` Does in Memory
questions.direct_answer: When you call `new Student()`, Java performs four steps in sequence: allocates space on the **heap** for all instance fields, fills them with default values, runs the constructor to set real values, then returns the heap address to the reference variable on the stack.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you understand the difference between stack (reference) and heap (object data), and the 4-step sequence that new triggers.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Thinking the object lives on the stack, or that the variable and the object are the same thing. The variable is just a pointer; the object is on the heap.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention that every object carries a hidden object header (metadata used by the JVM for garbage collection and type identification), so the actual memory footprint is slightly larger than just the fields.

sections.title: The Four Things `new` Does Every Time You Call It
sections.content:
When you call `new`, Java **builds an object in memory and hands you back its address**. That is the headline — and it happens in four small steps you can name.

Why does this matter? Because a variable like `s1` and the object it refers to are two different things living in two different places. **Knowing exactly what `new` does** is how you reason about why a change through one variable shows up in another, or why an object sometimes survives after you set the variable to `null`.

Here is the mechanism, one step at a time:

- First, **memory for the object is reserved on the heap** — the heap is the area of memory where Java keeps objects while the program runs. If a `Student` has a `name` and `marks`, the JVM (the engine that runs Java) sets aside room for both.
- Second, **every field is filled with its default value** — `null` for objects, `0` for numbers, `false` for booleans — so you never see leftover garbage from old memory.
- Third, **the constructor runs** and overwrites those defaults with the real values you passed in. The key insight here: the constructor does not create the object; the object already exists by step three — the constructor only initializes it.
- Fourth, **the heap address is returned** and stored into the reference variable on the **stack** (the fast, per-method area that holds local variables). From that moment, `s1` is just a pointer; the real data lives on the heap.

The interview nuance worth dropping in: every object also carries a hidden **object header** — a few bytes of metadata the JVM uses for garbage collection and to know the object's type — so an object always weighs slightly more than the sum of its fields.

The gotcha: `s1 = null` does **not** delete the object. It only drops the pointer. The object keeps sitting on the heap, unreachable, until the garbage collector eventually reclaims it.

> **Remember:** the object lives on the `heap` and the reference lives on the `stack` — the constructor initializes, it never creates.

sections.title: The 4-Step Sequence Every Time `new` Runs
sections.content:
```mermaid flowchart TD A["new Student(\"Alice\", 95)"] --> B["Step 1: JVM allocates
heap space for fields"] B --> C["Step 2: Fields default-filled
name=null, marks=0"] C --> D["Step 3: Constructor runs
name=Alice, marks=95"] D --> E["Step 4: Heap address returned
stored into s1 on the stack"] E --> F["s1 now points to
the live object on heap"] ``` The constructor runs *after* the object exists — its job is initialization, not creation.

sections.title: Stack vs Heap After `Student s1 = new Student()`
sections.content:
The variable lives on the stack; the object lives on the heap. They are connected by an address. ```mermaid flowchart LR subgraph Stack R["s1
= 0xA200"] end subgraph Heap O["Student @ 0xA200
name: \"Alice\"
marks: 95"] end R -->|"holds address of"| O ``` If you write `Student s2 = s1`, both `s1` and `s2` hold the address `0xA200` — there is still only ONE object on the heap. Changing `s2.marks` changes what `s1.marks` sees too.

sections.title: Watching the Four Steps — Default Fill, Then the Constructor
Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Thinking the object lives on the stack** — only the reference (the address) sits on the stack; the actual object data always lives on the heap, and confusing the two is the single most common error here.
- **Believing the constructor creates the object** — heap allocation and default-filling happen first; by the time the constructor runs the object already exists, and the constructor only sets its initial values.
- **Assuming `s1 = null` deletes the object** — it just removes one pointer; the object survives on the heap until no reference points to it and the garbage collector reclaims it.
- **Reading `Student s2 = s1` as a copy** — it copies the address, not the object, so both variables drive the same heap object and a change through one is visible through the other.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **`new` triggers 4 steps**: allocate heap → default-fill fields → run constructor → return address.
- **Object lives on the heap; reference lives on the stack** — they are not the same thing.
- **Default-fill happens before the constructor**: fields are never garbage values.
- **Constructor does not create the object** — it initializes an object that already exists in memory.
- **`s1 = null` does not destroy the object**: it just removes the pointer; the heap object waits for garbage collection.

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content:
I'd walk through it as **four steps**. When `new Student()` runs, Java first reserves space on the `heap` for the object's fields, then default-fills them — `null`, `0`, `false` — so you never get garbage. Then the constructor runs and sets your real values, and finally the heap address is handed back and stored in the reference variable on the `stack`.

The detail that shows you actually understand it is **the split**: the variable on the stack is just an address, while the real data sits on the heap. So `Student s2 = s1` doesn't make a second object — it copies the address, and now **two variables drive the same object**.

The point most people miss is that **the constructor doesn't create the object**; the object already exists by the time it runs, so the constructor only initializes it. And setting `s1 = null` never deletes anything — it drops the pointer and leaves the object for the garbage collector.

If I want to go one level deeper, every object also carries a **small hidden header** the JVM uses for GC and type info, so it always weighs a bit more than just its fields.

questions.question: What is the difference between a reference variable and the object it points to in Java?
questions.title: Reference Variable vs Object in Java
questions.direct_answer: A **reference variable** is a stack slot that stores the heap address of an object — it is the remote control. The **object** is the actual data (fields + methods) sitting on the heap — it is the TV. Multiple reference variables can point to the same object, and a reference can be `null` (pointing to nothing at all).

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you understand that a variable is not the object — it is just a pointer — and can reason about what happens when two variables point to the same object.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Treating `Student s1 = new Student()` as though `s1` IS the student. s1 is just the address. The real student data is on the heap.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Describe the two-variable-same-object scenario: `s2 = s1` means both variables point to the same heap object. Changing one changes what the other sees — there is no copy.

sections.title: The Remote Control and the TV: Why the Variable Isn't the Object
sections.content:
A reference variable is **the address of an object**, and the object is the actual data — they are two separate things. The variable points to the object; it is not the object itself.

Why does Java work this way? Objects can be large and you often need several names for the same one — passing an object into a method, storing it in a list, sharing it between parts of your program. Handing around a small address is cheap; copying the whole object every time would be slow and wasteful. So Java **keeps the object in one place and passes around pointers to it**.

Here is the picture that makes it click: a **reference variable** is like a TV remote, and the **object** is the TV. The remote isn't the TV — it just knows where the TV is and sends it commands. Write `Student s1 = new Student()` and `s1` is a remote (a small address sitting on the **stack**, the fast area for local variables) pointing at a Student that lives on the **heap** (where objects are stored). Hand a friend a second remote for the same TV with `Student s2 = s1`, and now two remotes control one TV. Do `s2.marks = 100` and `s1.marks` also reads `100` — because you changed the one shared object, not the remote. There was never a copy.

The nuance interviewers probe: because `s2 = s1` shares the object rather than copying it, comparing with `==` checks whether two remotes point at the **same** TV, not whether two TVs show the same picture. Two separate `new Student()` objects with identical fields are still `==` false.

The gotcha: **a reference can point at nothing**. `Student s3 = null` is a remote with no TV. Press a button on it — `s3.marks` — and you get a `NullPointerException`, the most common Java error, caused by using a reference that points to no object.

> **The rule:** the reference is the remote on the `stack`; the object is the TV on the `heap` — `==` compares remotes, `.equals()` compares pictures.

sections.title: Two References, One Object — and a Null Reference
sections.content:
```mermaid flowchart LR subgraph Stack S1["s1 = 0xA200"] S2["s2 = 0xA200"] S3["s3 = null"] end subgraph Heap O1["Student @ 0xA200
name: Alice, marks: 95"] NONE["(nothing)"] end S1 -->|"same object"| O1 S2 -->|"same object"| O1 S3 -.->|"points to nothing"| NONE ``` `s1` and `s2` are two remotes for one TV. `s3` is a remote with no TV — using it throws `NullPointerException`.

sections.title: Two References to One Object — Proof
Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Treating the variable as the object** — `s1` is only the address; the real Student data lives on the heap, and saying "`s1` is the student" hides every bug that comes from sharing.
- **Expecting `s2 = s1` to make a copy** — it copies the address, so both variables point at one object; modifying through `s2` is instantly visible through `s1`.
- **Comparing objects with `==`** — `==` checks whether two references hold the same address, not whether the objects have equal content; use `.equals()` for content, and two separate `new` objects are `==` false even with identical fields.
- **Calling a method on a `null` reference** — `s3.name` when `s3` is `null` throws `NullPointerException`; a declared reference is not an object until something is assigned to it.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Reference variable = address on the stack**. The object's data lives on the heap.
- **`s2 = s1` is not a copy** — both variables point to the same object. Changing via `s2` affects what `s1` sees.
- **`null` means no object** — the reference variable exists but points to nothing; calling any method on it gives `NullPointerException`.
- **`==` on objects compares addresses**, not content — two separate `new Student()` calls with the same field values will return `false` for `==`.
- **To copy an object**, you need to explicitly create a new one and copy fields — Java does not do shallow copy automatically.

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content:
The way I picture it is **a remote control and a TV**. The reference variable is the remote — a small address sitting on the `stack` — and the object is the TV, the real data on the `heap`. The remote isn't the TV; it just knows where it is.

That distinction matters because of what happens when you copy a reference. `Student s2 = s1` doesn't clone the object — it hands you a **second remote for the same TV**, so if I change something through `s2`, `s1` sees it immediately. There's only ever one object. That's also why a method can modify an object you pass in: it gets its own remote to your TV, not a copy.

The mistake I'd flag is comparing objects with `==` — that checks whether **two remotes point at the same TV**, not whether two TVs show the same picture, so for content you use `.equals()`.

And the famous one: a reference can be `null`, a remote with no TV, and pressing a button on it — calling a method — gives you a `NullPointerException`. So I never treat the variable as the object; **it's just a pointer to it**.

questions.question: What is the difference between instance members and static members in a Java class?
questions.title: Instance Members vs Static Members in Java
questions.direct_answer: **Instance members** (fields and methods without `static`) belong to each individual object — every `Student` has its own `name` and `marks`. **Static members** belong to the class itself — shared by all objects, accessible without creating an instance, and there is exactly one copy no matter how many objects exist.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you understand that instance members are per-object and static members are per-class, and know when to use each.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Using static for fields that should vary per object — e.g. making `name` static means all Students suddenly share one name. Also trying to access instance members from a static method (compile error).
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Give the classic static counter example: `static int count` incremented in the constructor gives you the total number of objects ever created, shared across all instances.

sections.title: Per-Object vs Per-Class: Who Owns the Data
sections.content:
An **instance member** belongs to each object separately, and a **static member** belongs to the class as a whole. The whole difference comes down to one question: who owns this piece of data?

Why have both? Some data is personal to each object — one student's `name` and `marks` have nothing to do with another's. But some data belongs to the type itself — like a running count of how many students have ever been created. You don't want that count copied into every object; you want one shared number. **That's exactly the line between instance and static.**

Here is how it works. **Instance members** are fields and methods written *without* the `static` keyword. Every object gets its own copy, so `s1.name` and `s2.name` are completely separate boxes. **Static members** are written *with* `static`, and there is exactly one copy for the entire class, shared by every object — you can even use it before any object exists, by writing `Student.count`. A good way to picture it: instance fields are like each student's own notebook, while a static field is a single whiteboard on the classroom wall that everyone reads and writes.

The classic interview move is the **static counter**: put `static int count = 0` in the class and write `count++` inside the constructor. Because the field is shared, every `new` bumps the same number — so `Student.count` tells you how many objects were ever created.

The gotcha that produces a compile error: **a static method cannot directly touch instance fields** or instance methods. A static method runs without any object, so there is no `this` — and if you reference `name` inside it, the compiler asks "which object's `name`?" and there is no answer.

> **Remember:** instance members are per-object (own copy); `static` members are per-class (one shared copy), and a `static` method has no `this`.

sections.title: Instance Members vs Static Members
sections.content:
| | Instance member | Static member |
|---|---|---|
| Declared with | No keyword | `static` keyword |
| Belongs to | Each individual object | The class itself |
| Memory | One copy per object | One copy for the entire class |
| Access | `objectRef.field` | `ClassName.field` or `objectRef.field` |
| Can access `this`? | Yes | No — no object context |
| Can be called without object? | No | Yes |
| Use for | Data that varies per object | Shared data, utility methods, constants |
| Example | `name`, `marks`, `printGrade()` | `count`, `Math.abs()`, `Integer.parseInt()` |

sections.title: Static Counter — One Value Shared Across All Objects
Memory Layout — Instance Fields per Object, Static Field Shared
sections.content:
```mermaid flowchart TD subgraph Class["Student class (method area)"] SF["static count = 3"] end subgraph Heap O1["s1 @ 0xA100
name: Alice
marks: 95"] O2["s2 @ 0xA200
name: Bob
marks: 72"] O3["s3 @ 0xA300
name: Carol
marks: 88"] end SF <-->|"shared — all objects
read & write same count"| O1 SF <-->|"shared"| O2 SF <-->|"shared"| O3 ``` `name` and `marks` are per-object — 3 objects = 3 copies. `count` is per-class — 3 objects, still just 1 copy.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Making per-object data `static`** — declare `name` as `static` and suddenly every student shares one name, so the last object created silently overwrites everyone else's value.
- **Accessing instance fields from a static method** — a static method has no `this`, so referencing `name` or `marks` inside it is a compile error, not a runtime surprise.
- **Reading static through an object reference** — `s1.count` compiles but misleads readers into thinking it's per-object; always use `Student.count` so it's clear the value belongs to the class.
- **Forgetting one static field is shared across all threads** — because there's a single copy, two threads incrementing `count` at once can lose updates; shared static mutable state needs synchronization.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Instance fields** — each object gets its own copy. `s1.name` and `s2.name` are completely separate.
- **Static fields** — one copy per class, shared by every object. `Student.count` is the same number wherever you read it.
- **Static methods cannot access instance members** — no `this` means no object context; the compiler will reject it.
- **Access static via class name**, not object reference: `Student.count` is clearer than `s1.count` even though both work.
- **Common static uses**: counters, constants (`static final int MAX = 100`), utility methods (`Math.abs()`, `Integer.parseInt()`).

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content:
It comes down to **ownership**. Instance members — anything without the `static` keyword — belong to each object, so every `Student` gets its own `name` and `marks`, and changing one student's doesn't touch another's. Static members belong to the class itself: there's exactly **one copy shared by everyone**, and you can use it without even creating an object, like `Student.count`.

The example I'd reach for is **a counter** — `static int count` with `count++` in the constructor — because it makes the shared nature obvious: every `new` bumps the same number, so the class knows how many objects exist.

The constraint worth naming is that a `static` method **can't directly touch instance fields**, because it runs without any object, so there's no `this` to say whose `name` you mean — that's a compile error, and it trips people up.

The deeper point is the **trap of overusing static**: the moment you make something shared mutable state, you've created one value that every object and every thread sees, which can quietly clobber data or race. So I keep `static` for genuinely class-wide things — counters, constants, utilities — and leave per-object data as instance fields.

speakable_v2.standard_example: Student with per-object name and marks plus a shared static count
speakable_v2.hook: **Instance members** belong to each object. **Static members** belong to the class itself. So instance data is per-object, while static is one shared copy for all.

groups.heading: Instance members
groups.text: Fields and methods without static. Each object gets its own copy, so one object's data doesn't touch another's.

groups.heading: Static members
groups.text: Marked static. There's one copy for the whole class, shared by every object and reachable as `Student.count`.

items: Use instance fields for anything that varies per object, like name and marks.
Use static for one shared thing, like a counter or a constant.
**The trap candidates miss**: a static method has no this, so it can't read instance fields.

beats.text: Put `static int count` in Student and bump it in the constructor. Every new object raises the same number, so `Student.count` tells how many exist. Names stay per-object.

speakable_v2.cap: So instance lives per-object with its own copy, while **static's** one shared copy per class. And a static **method's** got no this to work with.
